questions.question_text: A researcher investigates whether the amount of sleep a person gets affects their reaction time. Identify the independent variable.

options.text: Amount of sleep, because it occurs first and may cause a change in reaction time.
Reaction time, because it is the value being tested.
options.why: Confuses the variable being measured for a response with the independent variable that is set first.

options.text: Both are independent, since they are recorded together.
options.why: Fails to distinguish the two roles; every bivariate relationship still has one variable of each type.

options.text: Neither, because sleep and reaction time cannot be compared.
options.why: Wrongly claims the two variables have no relationship to identify roles for.

questions.solution_text:
Amount of sleep is set first and may lead to a change in reaction time.
Independent variable: **amount of sleep**.

questions.question_text: A cyclist studies whether pedalling speed affects the distance covered in a fixed time. Which variable should be plotted on the horizontal axis?

options.text: Pedalling speed — it is the independent variable, the possible cause.
Distance covered — because it is the final result of the graph.
options.why: Assumes the outcome of the relationship always belongs on the horizontal axis.

options.text: The fixed time — because it is mentioned in the question.
options.why: Treats a fixed control detail as if it were one of the two variables in the relationship.

options.text: Distance covered — because larger values usually go on the horizontal axis.
options.why: Bases axis choice on the size of the numbers rather than the variable's role.

questions.solution_text:
The horizontal axis holds the independent variable — the possible cause.
Pedalling speed is set and may lead to a change in distance covered.
**Pedalling speed** belongs on the horizontal axis.

questions.question_text: A study investigates whether the number of hours of sunlight a solar panel receives affects the electricity it generates. Which explanation correctly justifies treating hours of sunlight as the independent variable?

options.text: Hours of sunlight occurs first and may cause a change in the electricity generated.
Hours of sunlight is measured in a unit (hours), so it must be independent.
options.why: Assumes the type of unit a variable is measured in decides its role.

options.text: Hours of sunlight usually has smaller numerical values, so it is independent.
options.why: Bases the variable's role on the size of its numbers rather than cause and effect.

options.text: Electricity generated is independent because it is what the study is trying to find out.
options.why: Swaps the roles — the variable being investigated for a response is the dependent variable, not the independent one.

questions.solution_text:
Hours of sunlight is set by the weather/panel placement and occurs before the electricity is generated.
It may explain a change in electricity generated, so it is the independent variable.

questions.question_text: A survey records each customer's spending on movies and spending on video games in one year, to see whether the two are related. Why is it difficult to say which is the independent and which is the dependent variable here?

options.text: Neither spending amount clearly causes the other — both may simply reflect how much disposable income the customer has.
It isn't difficult — movie spending is always independent because it is listed first.
options.why: Assumes the order variables are listed in a sentence decides their role.

options.text: It isn't difficult — whichever amount is larger is the dependent variable.
options.why: Bases the variable's role on the size of the amount rather than cause and effect.

options.text: It is difficult only because both amounts are measured in dollars instead of a count.
options.why: Blames the ambiguity on the unit of measurement rather than the lack of a clear causal direction.

questions.solution_text:
Neither spending amount clearly happens first or causes the other — both could instead be explained by a customer's overall disposable income.
Without a believable cause-and-effect direction, the independent/dependent roles are not clear-cut here.

questions.question_text: It is thought that the amount of traffic on a road affects how long a bus takes to complete its route. Identify the dependent variable.

options.text: Time for the bus to complete its route — it is the possible effect, responding to the traffic level.
Amount of traffic — because it changes throughout the day.
options.why: Assumes a variable that changes a lot must be the dependent one.

options.text: Amount of traffic — because it is measured on the road the bus travels.
options.why: Confuses where a variable is measured with which role it plays in the relationship.

options.text: Both variables — because they are recorded on the same trip.
options.why: Fails to distinguish the two roles; being recorded together does not make both variables dependent.

questions.solution_text:
Traffic level occurs first and may lead to a change in how long the route takes.
Dependent variable: **time for the bus to complete its route**.

questions.question_text: A study graphs the number of advertisements a business shows against the number of enquiries it receives. Which variable belongs on the vertical axis?

options.text: Number of enquiries — it is the dependent variable, the possible effect.
Number of advertisements — because it is the variable deliberately changed to test its effect.
options.why: Correctly identifies the independent variable but places it on the wrong axis; the independent variable belongs on the horizontal axis.

options.text: Whichever variable has the larger axis values.
options.why: Bases axis assignment on the size of the numbers rather than the variable's role.

options.text: Number of advertisements — because it is recorded first in the study.
options.why: Mistakes the order data is recorded in for which axis a variable belongs on.

questions.solution_text:
The vertical axis holds the dependent variable — the possible effect.
Enquiries respond to the number of advertisements shown, so enquiries is the dependent variable.
**Number of enquiries** belongs on the vertical axis.
